paper_title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

sections.content: FAME-QP: GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control Santosh Mohan Rajkumar, Debdipta Goswami, and Stephanie Stockar AbstractWe present FAME-QP, GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused singleand two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance. I. INTRODUCTION Quadratic programming (QP) problems arise in wide range of applications, including statistics, machine learning, finance, and model predictive control (MPC) for robotic and control systems [1][3]. They also appear as subproblems in nonlinear optimization algorithms, such as sequential quadratic programming (SQP). Many of these applications lead to convex QP problems. Among these applications, MPC requires solving an optimization problem within each control sampling period, making computational efficiency critical for real-time operation [4]. With linear prediction models, convex quadratic costs, and linear constraints, each MPC update requires solving convex QP problem, yielding formulation commonly referred to as linear MPC (LMPC). Common solution approaches for QP problems include interior-point (IP), active-set (AS), operator-splitting (OS), and proximal methods. Representative IP methods include HPIPM [5], qpSWIFT [6], PIQP [7], and Clarabel [8] (with QP as special case). Although IP methods often converge in relatively few iterations, each iteration requires solving potentially expensive linear system. They are also generally more difficult to warm start, limiting their ability to exploit similarities between successive QP problems in MPC [9]. AS methods, such as qpOASES [10] and DAQP [11], readily support warm starting and can be highly efficient when initialized with the correct active set. However, their combinatorial worst-case complexity in the number of constraints can limit their scalability to large-scale QPs [9]. OS methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), such as OSQP [2], and related proximal methods, such as ProxQP [12], are increasingly used in robotic MPC owing to their ease of warm starting and suitability for applications requiring moderate solution accuracy [13], [14]. Authors are with the Department of Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA. E-mail:{rajkumar.36, goswami.78, stockar.1}@osu.edu Open Source Code: https://github.com/santoshrajkumar/fame-qp Moreover, their computational structure offers opportunities for parallelization. Nevertheless, their convergence rates can be slower than those of other methods, particularly when highaccuracy solutions are required [7]. Fig. 1: Cold-solve times on dense random QPs at matched accuracy, excluding setup. Lines show medians and bands minmax ranges across five instances, each timed by its median over repeated cold solves. All solvers use float64 except cuOSQP (float32). Although most established QP solvers are CPU-based, GPUs offer opportunities to accelerate large-scale QP solving through massive parallelism and higher memory bandwidth, enabling concurrent execution of independent computations and faster data movement [13]. Growing interest in MPC for robotics and control using world models [15], [16], locally linear latent dynamics [17], and Koopman-based linear, bilinear, or semi-linear representations [18][20] further motivates GPU acceleration to meet the real-time computational demands of large-scale MPCs. Moreover, modern robotics increasingly relies on GPUs for parallel simulation, inference, and learning [21][23]. Integrating CPU-native QP solvers into such pipelines can introduce additional latency through frequent CPUGPU data transfers [24]. Together, these considerations motivate GPU-native QP solvers that keep optimization data and computations on the device. This work presents FAME-QP, Fused ADMM with Multimode Execution for QP solution, GPU solver for the dense QPs of linear MPC. Its contributions are: (i) constraintdependent operator representations that reduce operator storage by up to 4 and iteration time by up to 3, relative to treating all constraint rows as dense; (ii) fused singleand two-kernel iterations with CUDA graph replay and automatic selection using device calibration and problem-specific timing; (iii) initial penalty selection through cached-operator probing and lazy operator updates for changing QP matrices; (iv) numerical and simulated robotic MPC evaluations demonstrating lower latency than the competing GPU methods evaluated in each benchmark, with matched solution accuracy on random QPs and comparable closed-loop control performance; and (v) an open-source implementation. A. Related Work GPU QP solvers. cuOSQP [13] parallelizes OSQP through linear solves, while qpax [25] and CuPIQP [26] indirect implement IP methods on GPUs, with CuPIQP exploiting kernel fusion and CUDA graph replay. The closest approach is ReLU-QP [9], which reformulates ADMM as weighttied neural network and caches pre-inverted operators for penalty adaptation. Its dense operator and repeated dispatch introduce computational and execution overhead, while its offline precomputation limits online matrix updates. FAME-QP retains the pre-inversion and penalty-bank approach but uses smaller, constraint-dependent operators, fused graph-replayed iterations, and lazy operator updates. GPU MPC solvers. MPCGPU [27] and TurboMPC [28] accelerate nonlinear MPC through GPU implementations of SQP and structured linear algebra. πMPC [29] exploits parallelism across the prediction horizon through consensus ADMM, while CUDA MPC [30] reduces execution overhead using persistent cooperative kernel and CUDA graphs. These methods exploit structure at the optimal-control level, whereas FAME-QP accepts dense convex QPs directly, including general constraint matrices and online matrix changes. Positioning. Our contribution lies in combining constraintdependent operator representations with automatic selection between fused singleand two-kernel iterations, initial penalty probing, and lazy matrix updates. The execution configuration is selected through device calibration and problem-specific timing, targeting the latency of individual MPC solves. II. PRELIMINARIES Notations. Define N0 := {0} N. We restrict attention to NVIDIA GPUs and the CUDA programming model [32]. GPU computations execute as kernels: functions typically launched by the host and executed in parallel by threads grouped into blocks [33]. Threads within block share fast on-chip memory and synchronize efficiently, while communication between blocks typically uses global memory. Successive kernels in the same stream execute in order, making kernel boundaries standard way to synchronize all blocks between computational stages [32]. CUDA graph represents workflow of GPU operations, such as kernel launches and data transfers, and the dependencies between them. The workflow is prepared once and can then be executed repeatedly with single host call, reducing host-side launch overhead [32]. When kernel is launched, its thread blocks are scheduled onto the GPUs streaming multiprocessors (SMs), where threads execute in groups of 32 called warps, using values held in registers. Global memory accesses may be served by GPU caches, while threads within block can exchange data through on-chip shared memory. Registers and shared memory have thread and block lifetimes, respectively, so intermediate results passed between kernels are typically stored in global memory [32]. The runtime of computation expressed as sequence of kernels therefore depends on arithmetic, data movement through the memory hierarchy, and launch and scheduling overhead. Kernel fusion combines operations that would otherwise execute in separate kernels into single kernel, allowing some intermediate results to remain in registers or shared memory. This can reduce both the number of kernel launches and global memory accesses [34]. A. Solving the QP with ADMM To solve (1), we employ the ADMM formulation proposed in [2]. With the stacked operator, one fused kernel computes and completes the iteration. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS We evaluate FAME-QP through numerical benchmarks and closed-loop robotic control experiments in high-fidelity MuJoCo simulations. The CPU QP baselines are OSQP [2], PIQP [7], ProxQP [12], Clarabel [8], and DAQP [11]. The GPU baselines include the QP solvers cuOSQP [13], ReLU-QP [9], qpax [25], and CuPIQP [26], and the MPC solvers CUDA MPC [30] and πMPC [29]. We use the original implementations, except for CUDA MPC, which we reimplement because its source code was unavailable. All experiments run on system equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 3080 Laptop GPU (48 SMs, 16 GB VRAM) and an Intel Core i7-11850H processor with 32 GB RAM. Unless stated otherwise, FAME-QP runs in float64 with σ = 106, α = 1.6, ϵabs = ϵrel = ϵ for stated tolerance ϵ, jchk = 10, and jmax = 2 104 (105 in the closed-loop random-LMPC and Unitree G1 experiments), with penalty adaptation and probing enabled; lazy updates are used where the QP matrices change at every step (KQ-LMPC). A. Numerical Experiments: Random QP and LMPC Dense random QPs. We use the dense random QPs of [9], with n/4 dense equality rows and n/4 dense one-sided inequality rows (approximately 30% of the inequalities active), using five random seeds per problem size n. To match solution accuracy across solvers, we sweep each solvers tolerance over {103, . . . , 108} and select the loosest value yielding an ℓ solution error of at most 103 on all five instances, relative to Clarabel solutions computed at tolerance 1010. We report the mean across instances of their median solve times. FAME-QP is set up, including penalty probing, on held-out instance of the same size. Setup time is excluded for all solvers; only solve time is reported. Figure 1 shows the median across five instances of their per-instance median cold-solve times, with minmax bands. Using the mean of these per-instance medians for numerical comparisons, FAME-QP in float64 outperforms all GPU baselines at every tested size and all CPU baselines for 220. Over = 2201400, its speedups are 1.225.9 over DAQP and 1.54.3 over ReLU-QP, the best CPU and competing GPU baselines, respectively. Since cuOSQPs native implementation uses float32, we also evaluate FAME-QP in this precision under the same accuracy criterion. Single precision further reduces its solve time at most sizes, although float64 remains faster at = 600 and 800. At = 1400, the mean solve time is 1.95 ms in float32, compared with 5.01 ms in float64 and 326 ms for cuOSQP. GPU LMPC on random systems. Following [9], we consider random unstable linear systems with nu {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}, nx = 3nu, spectral radius 1.05, and horizon = 40, with = I, = 0.1I, an LQR terminal cost, and input bounds 1. Initial states are chosen so that input bounds are active on at least 30% of the steps under exact MPC. We compare FAME-QP with ReLU-QP and CuPIQP, the two fastest GPU QP baselines in the random-QP benchmark, and with the GPU MPC methods CUDA MPC and πMPC. The QP solvers receive the same LQR pre-stabilized condensed QP (n = 40nu); the MPC methods receive the original OCP. Each method runs 50 closed-loop steps in float64 after one untimed solve at x0. Timings exclude setup and the initialization solve but include data updates, warm-start shifts, and transfer of the first input to the host. and Table shows that FAME-QP achieves the lowest mean step time at every size, from 0.658 to 4.23 ms. Ablation Study We isolate GPU execution, constraint structure, operator selection, penalty probing, and matrix updates. Fixed-budget experiments time 200 iterations at fixed penalty without termination checks; complete solves include convergence checks and transfer of the solution to the host. Within each comparison, the problem data and all other settings are identical. Fusion and graph replay. We compare separate operations and fused kernels, each with ordinary launches or CUDA graph replay, on the same stacked operator with mc = n/4. Table III shows that the two are complementary: at = 128, replay reduces the unfused iteration time from 140 to 24.6 µs and fusion further to 4.37 µs, replacing 14 kernels per iteration with one. The gain shrinks as the operator grows and the matrixvector product dominates. All variants produce the same iterates to within 3 1010. Constraint structure. For QPs with = [I; C], mc {0, n/4, n}, and both operator forms, we compare treating every row as dense against extracting the diagonal rows. Extraction reduces operator storage by 1.674.00 and iteration time by 1.073.03, with unchanged iteration counts and solutions (within 1012). At = 512 and mc = 128, the stacked operator shrinks from 10.1 to 3.12 MiB and the iteration time from 49.8 to 17.3 µs, whereas ReLU-QPs (n + 2m)2 operator needs 24.5 MiB and 86.3 µs under the same graph replay; overall, it is 1.65.8 slower per iteration than the extracted operator. Automatic operator selection. We sweep mc from 16 to 1024 for {128, 512, 1028} and compare the stacked, factored, and automatically selected forms. Automatic selection picks the faster form at 30 of 36 points; the six misses fall within the 10% retention margin of Sec. III-E, and the selected configuration is at most 9.5% slower than the faster fixed form, whereas always stacking or always factoring is up to 2.2 or 1.5 slower. Pruning never excludes the faster form, but the model alone misplaces the crossover by about factor of two, hence the final choice by measured timings. Penalty probing. To separate the starting penalty from bank re-centering, we compare default and probed starts on the dense random QPs, with one bank spanning both ranges. At tolerance 105, the probed start reduces iterations by 1.63.2 and complete-solve time by 1.43.3 (Table III); widening the bank alone changes iteration counts by at most 5%. separate run crosses unfused and fused iterations with and without the full probe (start and re-centered bank). Iteration counts do not depend on fusion, so the gains multiply: from = 250 to 1000, fusion contributes 2.00 falling to 1.26 and the probe 1.40 rising to 3.35, for 2.84.2 combined, with the setup cost recovered after about 36122 solves. Probed FAME-QP and default ReLU-QP reach 103 accuracy in similar iteration counts (3038 versus 3032), so the speedup over ReLU-QP stems mainly from per-iteration cost. For split constraints, we replay recorded quadrotor KQLMPC sequence (N = 50) whose QP matrices change at every step. Probing ρ lowers the median and tail step times relative to the default penalty; probing γ as well leaves the median essentially unchanged but further shortens the tail and nearly eliminates in-solve penalty switches. Lazy matrix updates. In KQ-LMPC, and change at every step, so the pre-inverted operators must be rebuilt before each solve. Replaying the recorded quadrotor QPs with identical data and warm starts, we compare full refresh, which re-inverts all five bank entries at every step, with lazy refresh, which re-inverts only the active entry and the others when penalty switch selects them. Full refresh makes the update, not the iterations, the dominant cost of step; lazy refresh roughly halves the update and median step times and shortens the tail, with identical iteration counts, solutions equal to numerical precision, and unchanged closed-loop tracking error. V. CONCLUSION FAME-QP accelerates dense MPC quadratic programs through constraint-dependent operators, fused GPU execution with automatic configuration selection, penalty probing, and lazy matrix updates. Numerical and simulated robotic experiments demonstrate reduced latency while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance, including with changing prediction matrices.
